newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: US envoy still hopeful of peaceful Zaire transition.
newsitem.headline: US envoy still hopeful of peaceful Zaire transition.

text.p: Bill Richardson, U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, said on Friday he still believed a peaceful transition in Zaire was possible but that any new government would likely be headed by rebel leader Laurent Kabila.
He said a peaceful handover would require another face-to-face meeting between Kabila and Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko "probably in the Congo" in the middle of next week.
He did not say if it would be on land or at sea following reports that a second meeting between the two would again be on a South African navy ship.
He confirmed reports Mobutu would return home first from the Gabonese capital of Libreville where he met leaders from francophone African states that support him.
Richardson was interviewed on public television's Newshour with Jim Lehrer shortly after he returned from Paris following shuttle diplomacy throughout Central Africa.
"I don't think a peaceful transition is dead yet," Richardson said, referring to diplomatic plans formulated by South African officials and U.N. envoy Mohammed Sahnoun.

"A lot of posturing takes place," he said. "I believe that Mobutu will return to Kinshasa before he heads for the Congo. I believe he is putting his affairs in order. But eventually I do believe there's still a good chance of a peaceful inclusive transition government."
He said Kabila would "most likely" head any transitional government in light of his military victories but that the transitional phase should include various factions.
"The big issue is going to be how much of Mobutu's people, if any at all, are part of that," he said.

Giving his impressions of Mobutu, Richardson said the president had not been "facing reality" and had been told by his advisers that "he could still hang on," despite the nearly hopeless military situation throughout the country.
"Unfortunately I was the bearer of a lot of bad news but nonetheless, I believe that Mobutu is now realistic. He is a dignified person. He wants to go out gracefully.
"He is bitter at the United States and some of its other allies for not backing him but the reality is that he's lost support in Kinshasa and throughout the country," he said.
As for Kabila, he said the rebel leader was "very street smart" and pragmatic. But he noted "he's never governed anything -- overwhelmed by the attention and the responsibility it takes."

Richardson warned Kabila that he needed to make sure his troops stopped mistreating Rwandan refugees and punished those responsible for refugee massacres in eastern Zaire if he wanted respect from the international community.
"He is going to need private investment and international assistance to survive, because literally Zaire right at this moment is falling apart," Richardson said.
"If he doesn't appear to be handling it in a humane way, he is not going to get help from the international cummunity. In fact he will become a pariah."

He said Kabila, whose troops have captured most of the country and were circling Kinshasa, the capital, would face little resistance if he behaved responsibly. "Otherwise there will be looting and chaos" mainly by Mobutu's soldiers.
Richardson also said the Angolans needed to "step aside ... They've got, unfortunately, some negative intentions in terms of moving their troops into Zaire to pay back Mobutu."

He was referring to Mobutu's support from Angolan UNITA rebel leader, Jonas Savimbi. "The Angolan government, which is in power now, wants to pay him back and they don't want to help Mobutu. They want him out militarily."
There have been numerous reports of both government and UNITA troops in Angola but Richardson sidestepped specific questions on the soldiers.
